name: Newberry & Dole's Forwarding and Commission Warehouse
aka: Newberry and Dole's Forwarding and Commission House

documented_range.note: THE TRADE IS DOCUMENTED FROM NOVEMBER 1833 AND THE BUILDING IS NOT DATED AT ALL. The range opens in November 1833 because that is the first contemporary evidence this project holds that the firm was doing this business in this town: the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries 'NEWBERRY & DOLE, Forwarding & Commission MERCHANTS' as a paid advertisement, and Andreas's summary of the paper's early advertising columns lists the same firm in the same trade (scan p. 755). An advertisement proves a trade was carried on and does not prove a building, which the source record for the Democrat states in as many words. The second fixed point is better for a warehouse: on 12 July 1834 the schooner Illinois, the first vessel through the new cut, was cheered at 'Newberry & Dole's wharf' (Andreas scan p. 503, via docs/research/04-structures-south.md), and a wharf of one's own with a name on it implies premises behind it. So a warehouse existed by the summer of 1834, twelve months before the scene date. THE 1838-39 NORTH-BANK GRAIN WAREHOUSE IS A DIFFERENT BUILDING AND IS DELIBERATELY OUTSIDE THIS RANGE — see the position note and data/exclusions.json's treatment of later structures. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim.

change_note: The warehouse as it stood in the river trade of 1834 and 1835. Nothing dates its building or describes any change to it, so the single phase is the shape of the evidence rather than a claim that the building stood still.

placement.position_note: THE BANK IS CONFLICTED IN THIS PROJECT'S OWN DOSSIERS AND THIS RECORD DOES NOT PRETEND TO SETTLE IT. READING A, THE SOUTH BANK, ADOPTED HERE: docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 3.10 reports 'a square frame building on South Water Street, "Newberry and Dole's Forwarding and Commission House", in views of c. 1835 — i.e., the south bank at that date', tagged [DOC]; that dossier names no source record for the views, which is why this record cannot cite them and why the reading is carried as inference rather than attestation. READING B, THE NORTH BANK: Andreas, 'It was made by Newberry & Dole, whose warehouse was on the North Side, immediately east of where Rush-street bridge now stands' (scan p. 1139), and docs/research/04-structures-south.md turns that into an explicit instruction — 'Do not put it on South Water Street.' WHY THE SOUTH BANK IS ADOPTED, STATED AS REASONING AND NOT AS PROOF: Andreas's sentence is not about 1835. Read in place it describes the warehouse from which a named grain shipment was made — the paragraph runs 'The history of the next shipment, in 1839, of three thousand six hundred and seventy-eight bushels, on board the brig "Osceola" ... It was made by Newberry & Dole, whose warehouse was on the North Side' — so the building it locates is the firm's warehouse in 1839, four years after the scene date, in a decade when the firm plainly moved and grew. The c. 1835 view evidence is contemporaneous with the scene and the Andreas sentence is not, so the south bank is the better reading FOR THIS DATE while remaining the weaker citation. A READER SHOULD KNOW THE MODELLING CONSEQUENCE TOO, AND THAT IT IS NOT A REASON: the Rush Street site lies about 1 km east of the datum origin, which in August 2026 was some 700 m beyond the modelled terrain box, so reading B would THEN have put the building outside modelled ground. That consequence has lapsed: the heightfield was extended east on 2026-08-11 to local E -320..+1700 and there is traced ground at the Rush Street site now (corrected 2026-08-22 under T-0010). That did not decide the choice and is recorded so nobody has to wonder whether it did. THE BLOCK IS UNATTESTED UNDER EITHER READING. South Water Street ran the length of the south bank and nothing says where on it this house stood, so the coordinate is a point chosen on a street: local E +200 to +211, at the west end of the frontage, clear of the seven South Water buildings this dataset already places between local E +257 and +724, with the north face about 8 m back from the traced bank to leave the dock its ground. That is free choice within a documented street, and it is why this position is conjectural and not inferred. Facade bearing 0, due north onto the river and its dock — a forwarding house faces its wharf — which is an argument from the trade, not a source.
placement.symbolic_location: South bank of the main stem, on the South Water Street river frontage west of the built-up blocks, with its dock on the water. THE BANK IS DISPUTED — see the note; the north bank is the other reading and is not adopted here.

footprint.note: THE SHAPE CARRIES EVIDENCE AND THE SIZE DOES NOT, which is the same distinction miller_house's footprint note draws and it should not be blurred. What is reported is a SQUARE frame building (docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 3.10, from views of c. 1835), so the polygon is square on purpose rather than by chance; the 11 m, about 36 ft on a side, is invented outright. The polygon cites no sources because the dossier's description of the views names none. To resolve: identify and read the c. 1835 view the dossier is describing — the candidates are the Blanchard & Shober 1867 'Wolf's Point in 1833' chromolithograph, the Chicago History Museum's early South Water Street drawings, and the Edgar S. Cameron painting of South Water Street; every one of them is retrospective, so even a positive identification gives a proportion rather than a measurement.

construction.note: 'a square FRAME building' in the c. 1835 views reported by docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 3.10. The dossier tags that [DOC] and names no source record, so this project cannot cite it and carries the reading as inference until the view is identified. `light_frame` is the archetype's term for boards laid horizontally on a stick frame, which is what a frame building looks like at this level of detail; what is behind the boards is not visible and is not claimed.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 3.4 m is about 11 ft at the eave — a tall single storey with storage in the roof, which is the working arrangement of a forwarding and commission house: goods in at ground level off the dock, stored above. Stated rather than left to the archetype's size-aware default of 4.1 m for a footprint this size, which would read as a full two storeys and would be a claim. The firm's LATER warehouse is described hoisting wheat 'to the upper story by Irish power, with rope and pully' (Andreas scan p. 1139) — that is the 1839 building, so it supports the practice and says nothing about this one.

door.note: No source describes an opening. 'wagon' is the archetype's widest doorway, a clear 2.9 m for a loaded team, and it is what a forwarding and commission business needs: the whole trade is taking goods off wagons and boats and putting them back on. A narrower door would say the house was a shop.

loft.note: Not attested for this building. A forwarding warehouse stores above the floor it loads on, and the archetype builds exactly one external trace of that — the door goods are hoisted through, high in a gable end — and nothing else: no dormer, no floor line, no second range of windows. Andreas's description of the firm's 1839 warehouse hoisting wheat to the upper storey is the practice this infers from, four years the wrong side of the scene date.

dock.note: DRAWN NOW, ON THE WHARF LAYER, AND EVERY DIMENSION OF IT IS RECONSTRUCTED. What is stated remains what it always was: the dossier's phrase for both river warehouses is 'each had a warehouse with its dock along the river front' (docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 3.10), and Andreas independently names 'Newberry & Dole's wharf' as the place the schooner Illinois was cheered on 12 July 1834 (scan p. 503). Nothing anywhere gives its length, width, height or construction. Until 2026-08-18 this attribute therefore declared geometry: 'absent' and a visitor saw a warehouse standing back from a bare bank, which understated the site — the dock is the half of it that made the building worth building. T-0041 draws it: data/wharves/river_landings.json, generated by tools/generate_river_wharves.py from the traced 1834 bank, this record's own footprint and the committed heightfield, and drawn at load by renderers/web/js/wharves.js. THE DECLARATION IS NOW 'simplified' AND THAT IS THE EXACT CLAIM: a reconstructed wharf of standard form stands in the place of this attribute, and the attribute's own value — true — is all of it that comes from evidence. Every metre of the outline is invented within stated bounds and claimed at docs/LIBERTIES.md L132; the deck's HEIGHT is neither invented nor stated but sampled from the terrain at load.

function.note: 'NEWBERRY & DOLE, Forwarding & Commission MERCHANTS' — the firm's own paid advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833, the first contemporary document in this dataset and about as good as evidence of a trade gets, since the advertiser was paying for it and his customers had to be able to find him. Andreas's summary of the paper's advertising columns lists the same firm in the same words (scan p. 755). Forwarding and commission is the lake trade: taking goods off vessels, holding them, and sending them on inland, on commission. The firm's wharf received the schooner Illinois, the first vessel through the new harbour cut, on 12 July 1834 (Andreas scan p. 503).

occupants.value: George W. Dole and Walter L. Newberry, trading as Newberry & Dole
occupants.note: THE FIRM IS DOCUMENTED AND THE PARTNER WAS MIS-ATTRIBUTED; T-0396 IS THE RULING (2026-09-12). This field read 'Oliver Newberry and George W. Dole' at `attested` on Andreas's packing-house chapter (scan p. 1151). Andreas is wrong on the Newberry, and the firm's own paid advertisement is what says so. IN EVERY SETTING OF THE NEWBERRY & DOLE CARD THAT NAMES OLIVER NEWBERRY HE STANDS IN ITS REFERENCE LIST, UNDER DETROIT — 'Oliver Newberry, [Det]roit' (Chicago Democrat, 1 April 1834, claim chicago_democrat_1834_04_01#c013) and 'OLIVER NKWBERRY, Detroit.' (1 July 1835, chicago_democrat_1835_07_01#c015) — one correspondent per port, beside Coenties Slip in New York, Barker & Holt of Buffalo, Calvin Britain at the mouth of the St Joseph and James B. Campbell at Ottawa. Both claims' own entity blocks give his role as a reference named in the advertisement, and neither gives him a trade. A house does not print its own resident partner as the man to write to in another city. THE SETTING OF 5 AUGUST 1835 (chicago_democrat_1835_08_05#c022) HOLDS BOTH MEN AT ONCE, which is what makes this a decision and not a preference: its partner entity reads 'NEWRERRY' at the trade of forwarding and commission merchant, while 'Oliver Newb[err]y, Detro[it]' still stands in the same card's reference list. THE TWO LIMBS ARE GRADED SEPARATELY, and the weaker one sets the confidence of the whole attribute. That Oliver Newberry was NOT the Chicago partner rests on the firm's own contemporary card against a compiler writing in 1884. WHICH Newberry he was is INFERRED: Fergus's directory of 1839 prints 'Newberry, Walter L., att'y and real est., office Newberry & Dole' — the firm's office as his office; the Chicago American of 8 June 1835 prints 'W. L. NEWBERRY' over the great sale of town lots and sets 'NEWBERRY & DOLE' over the same date in the adjacent column of the same issue; and no other Newberry forename is printed for Chicago anywhere in this corpus. The firm style is unbroken from 26 November 1833 to 5 August 1835 and no printing records a change of partner, so the ruling reaches across this record's whole range rather than only the scene date. THE ONE RIVAL LEFT UNRESOLVED IS NOT A PRINTING: the land register's WALTER S / W S, read at data/research/land_sales/README.md § The two Newberrys the register writes. The ruling itself is declared at data/research/newspapers/identity.json § proprietor_distinctions, which is where the corpus put the question. The value records whose business it was, not who was on the premises on any day — unchanged by this ruling, which changes WHO the business was.

persons.name: George Washington Dole
persons.note: TOWN TREASURER TWICE AND TRUSTEE TWICE - the most continuously documented office-holder in the dataset. Elected trustee 10 August 1833 with 26 of 28 votes (tied top of the poll with Owen), appointed town treasurer at the board's first business meeting on 4 September 1833, and elected trustee AND treasurer again at the third town election of July 1835 (Andreas, scan pp. 273, 369). He is therefore in office on the scene date on the face of the record. Also a provision packer: this dataset holds two slaughtering and packing buildings under his name. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Dole, George W.” (poll_1833_010, line 31); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Dole, George W.” (tax_1833_025, line 77); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Dole, George W.” (poll_1834_034, line 203). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Dole' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the city register of 1839 — “George W. Dole” as treasurer (f1839_r0005, printed page 38). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes_date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches_scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Dole' folds to the same string as the register entry's, and the given name of both begins G. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 4 times, as “DOLE GEORGE W”, 1833-10-22 to 1833-10-24: 4 parcels of the school section — BL73 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL75 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; lot 3 of block 2 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 6 of block 2 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 9.07 acres stated in all, for $500.50 (ls0147, ls0148, ls0149, ls0150). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: DOLE GEORGE W matches George Washington Dole: the forename names George Washington Dole of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Geo. W. Dole” (33SQ-GYYJ-RJ, printed page 233, line 12). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (L6 matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (data/research/census_1840/resident_crosswalk.json). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Dole, George W. | Letter. | June I, 1842. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0537, printed page 184), admitted 1842-06-01 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Dole' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins G. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

residents.research_note: THE BEST-DOCUMENTED BUSINESSMAN IN THE 1835 TOWN and the household that shows what the sources do and do not give. The trade, the partnership, the buildings and the public offices are all attested, some of them contemporaneously. The man's arrival year, his family, his origin and his address are not attested at all. THE NEWBERRY HALF OF THE FIRM IS A CHICAGO HOUSEHOLD, AND IT IS NOT OLIVER'S (T-0396, 2026-09-12 — this paragraph read the other way round until then): the firm's own advertisement prints Oliver Newberry in its REFERENCE LIST under Detroit, beside its New York, Buffalo, St Joseph and Ottawa correspondents, and the card of 5 August 1835 prints him there alongside a partner read as 'NEWRERRY'. The Chicago Newberry of the style is inferred to be Walter L. Newberry, whose household this layer already holds at hh_newberry_walter_loomis. Oliver Newberry stays out, and on a better reason than before: the bill of lading Andreas prints names 'O. Newberry, Detroit', and Andreas describes him throughout as Oliver Newberry of Detroit, builder of the steamer Michigan. He is recorded in data/residents/index.json among the people researched and NOT made residents, which is the honest place for a correspondent whose home port was the other end of the route — 'partner' is the word that paragraph used to carry, and it is the word the ruling took away.

research_note: THIS RECORD EXISTS TO CARRY A DISAGREEMENT, NOT TO END ONE, AND THE POSITION NOTE IS WHERE THE DISAGREEMENT LIVES. Two of this project's own dossiers put Newberry & Dole's warehouse on opposite banks of the Chicago River and one of them says in as many words 'Do not put it on South Water Street'. The building is placed on the south bank, the position is tagged conjectural, and the reasoning is written out with both citations so a later reader can overturn it on the evidence rather than on the shape of the file. THE ONE THING THAT MOVED THE ARGUMENT IN THIS SLICE was reading Andreas's north-bank sentence in place: it sits inside an account of a grain shipment made in 1839 on the brig Osceola, so the warehouse it locates is the firm's warehouse four years after the scene date. That does not make the south bank right; it makes the north-bank citation the wrong date rather than the wrong place. THREE BUILDINGS MUST BE KEPT APART and this dataset now holds all three: dole_warehouse_south, George W. Dole's 1832 warehouse and slaughter yard near the later Tremont House site; newberry_dole_slaughterhouse_south_branch, the firm's 1834 killing and packing plant; and this one, the forwarding and commission house on the river. A fourth — the 1838-39 grain warehouse and elevator on the north bank east of Rush Street, the one that made Chicago's first grain shipments — is LATER THAN THE SCENE and must not be modelled; it is the building Andreas's north-bank sentence describes. WHAT WOULD RESOLVE THE BANK: identifying the c. 1835 view the dossier reports and giving it a source record; or any Chicago Democrat advertisement of 1834-35 carrying the firm's street address, which is exactly the kind of evidence the paper's advertising columns supply and exactly the reason more of the paper should be read into this dataset.
